name: Umami
statement: Beyond sweet, sour, salty, and bitter lies a fifth taste: the savoury depth of broth and cheese.
statementAccent: the savoury depth of broth and cheese
meaning: Umami is one of the five basic tastes, alongside sweet, sour, salty, and bitter. It is the savoury, brothy, meaty taste characteristic of broths, cooked meats, aged cheeses, and many other foods, and its name comes from a Japanese word meaning, roughly, pleasant savoury taste. Umami is produced chemically by glutamate, an amino acid whose salt monosodium glutamate, or MSG, is a familiar seasoning, together with certain nucleotides, particularly inosinate and guanylate. A striking feature of umami is synergy: when glutamate is combined with these nucleotides, the resulting savoury intensity is far greater than the sum of the two alone. Umami was first scientifically identified in 1908 by the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda, who isolated glutamate from kombu seaweed broth and coined the term, then developed MSG as a seasoning. Once controversial, umami is now widely accepted as a genuine fifth basic taste, detected by dedicated taste receptors, and it is central to cooking around the world.
mechanism: Umami is the taste of glutamate, specifically the free glutamate present in foods, detected by taste receptors on the tongue that respond to it, including receptors formed from taste receptor type 1 proteins and related glutamate receptors. This detection of glutamate as a distinct quality, separate from the other four basic tastes, is what qualifies umami as a fifth basic taste. The savoury sensation is greatly amplified by synergy with ribonucleotides: foods rich in glutamate become far more intensely umami when combined with ingredients containing inosinate or guanylate, so the taste of the combination is stronger than adding the two would predict. This is why classic pairings, such as the Japanese dashi broth of kombu, rich in glutamate, with bonito flakes, rich in inosinate, or the combination of Parmesan cheese with tomatoes and mushrooms, taste so deeply savoury. Ikeda discovered the phenomenon by isolating glutamate from kombu seaweed, and the industrial seasoning MSG delivers concentrated glutamate to reproduce and enhance the umami taste.

examples.text: Umami comes from glutamate, as in MSG, together with the nucleotides inosinate and guanylate found in meats, fish, and mushrooms.
Combining a glutamate-rich food with a nucleotide-rich one, as in kombu and bonito dashi, multiplies the umami far beyond their sum.
Aged cheeses like Parmesan, tomatoes, mushrooms, cured meats, fish, soy sauce, miso, and seaweed are all rich in umami.

variants.name: The synergy effect
variants.text: The multiplication of umami intensity when glutamate is combined with the nucleotides inosinate or guanylate.

variants.name: Monosodium glutamate
variants.text: The seasoning MSG, developed by Ikeda, that delivers concentrated glutamate to produce and enhance the umami taste.

whyItMatters: Umami is a fundamental concept in taste science and cooking, expanding the classic four basic tastes to five and giving a name to the savoury depth that makes so many foods satisfying. Recognizing umami as a distinct basic taste, detected by specific receptors, reshaped the understanding of how humans perceive flavour and vindicated Kikunae Ikeda's early insight. In the kitchen, umami is central to the appeal of broths, stocks, roasted and cured meats, aged cheeses, tomatoes, mushrooms, and fermented foods like soy sauce and miso, and understanding it, especially the synergy between glutamate and nucleotides, helps cooks build deeply savoury, satisfying dishes. Umami also underlies the use of seasonings like MSG and explains why certain ingredient combinations taste so much richer together. Beyond cooking, umami connects to nutrition and appetite, since glutamate signals protein-rich food. As the savoury fifth taste, once doubted and now established, umami is essential to how we experience and create flavour worldwide.

working.text: supply foods rich in free glutamate, such as broths, aged cheeses, tomatoes, or the seasoning MSG.
let taste receptors that respond to glutamate register the distinct savoury quality of umami.
combine glutamate with inosinate- or guanylate-rich ingredients to multiply the umami through synergy.

limits: Umami is now widely accepted as a fifth basic taste, but its recognition took most of a century after Ikeda's 1908 discovery, and the precise identity and workings of the umami taste receptors remain an area of ongoing scientific detail. Umami describes the savoury taste of glutamate and related compounds, not the whole of a food's flavour, which also involves aroma, the other tastes, and texture. The synergy effect is real but depends on the specific combination and amounts of glutamate and nucleotides. Cultural attitudes to umami and to MSG have varied, with past unfounded fears about MSG, so perceptions do not always match the science. So umami robustly names the savoury fifth taste produced by glutamate and enhanced by nucleotides, understood as one component of flavour whose receptor details are still being refined.
misreadings: Umami is not simply saltiness or a flavour enhancer's trick; it is a distinct basic taste, the savoury quality of glutamate, separate from sweet, sour, salty, and bitter. It is not produced only by MSG, since glutamate occurs naturally in cheeses, tomatoes, mushrooms, and broths. And the fears once attached to MSG are not supported by evidence, so treating umami as mere saltiness, as artificial, or as harmful, misreads a genuine fifth taste that signals the savoury depth of glutamate-rich food.
origin: First scientifically identified in 1908 by the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda, who isolated glutamate from kombu broth, coined the term, and developed MSG; one of the five basic tastes.
